text:
**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, get a power station with about 1,400-2,000 Wh of capacity (enough for roughly 24 hours) and a surge rating of at least 1,300 W. A ~1,000 Wh unit covers about half a day to most of a day.

## Three numbers to check

1. **Surge watts (the one that most often fails):** the compressor spikes at startup. Sources put this at roughly 1,000-1,300 W for typical fridges and up to 2,400 W for large or older ones. Look for a surge rating of at least 1,300 W, and higher if your fridge is big or old. ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))
2. **Continuous watts:** a running fridge draws about 100-250 W, so almost any 1,000 W-class station covers this. Add up anything else you plan to run at the same time.
3. **Watt-hours:** the compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time. One estimate for a typical ENERGY STAR fridge is about 41 W average, or around 1,400 Wh per day after inverter losses and headroom. A large side-by-side with an ice maker can use about twice that. ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator))

Also look for a **pure sine wave** inverter, which is better for compressor motors.

## Rough capacity guide

| Outage length | Capacity |
|---|---|
| ~12-17 hours | ~1,000 Wh |
| 24 hours | ~1,400-2,000 Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800 Wh or more |

For a precise number, take your fridge's yearly kWh from its EnergyGuide label, multiply by 1,000, and divide by 8,760 to get average watts. Then multiply by the hours you need, divide by 0.85 for inverter losses, and add about 20% headroom. Keeping the door closed helps a lot.

## Options from these results

- **BLUETTI AC200L (2,048 Wh, 2,400 W, 3,600 W Power Lifting, LiFePO4):** a good 24-hour-plus fit that can expand up to 8 kWh. It's $899, or $854.05 with code AFF5OFF, which the Dealectric affiliate site says it tested in BLUETTI's cart. [Buy at BLUETTI](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) ([details](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l))
- **Anker SOLIX S2000 (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W, 3,000 W peak, pure sine wave):** listed at $699.99 after coupon. [Anker SOLIX page](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (~1,070 Wh, about $499):** a budget pick that runs a fridge about 17 hours in HomeGrid HQ's estimate, so it falls short of a full day. [Listed here](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)
- **BLUETTI AC180 / AC180P (1,152 / 1,440 Wh, 2,700 W peak):** BlackBox's top pick. The 1,440 Wh AC180P just meets the 24-hour target in powerstations.reviews' math, but it was sold out at the maker's site when they checked. [BlackBox](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)

I couldn't see a direct purchase link for every model in the results, so for the Jackery and AC180 you'll need to use the listing pages above. Prices and stock change, so confirm at checkout. These guide sites earn affiliate commissions.

If you tell me your fridge's size or its kWh/year label, plus how long an outage you want to cover, I can narrow this to one pick.
